$comment: Capability -> runner label. A job says what it needs; this file says what
answers today. Read by scripts/ci/resolve_runners.py, published by
.github/workflows/resolve-runners.yml. See docs/ci-runner-capability-map.md.
Every fleet must define every capability key. A fleet missing a key would
emit an empty runs-on, and an empty or unknown label does not error on
GitHub: the job sits queued forever and holds its concurrency group. The
resolver refuses to start on a fleet with a missing key for that reason.
Capability keys are requirements, not lanes. Who is asking (pull request,
manual flake hunt, non-urgent background work) is cost policy and is not
expressed here.

capabilities.linux: x86_64 Linux; the default for every non-macOS job
capabilities.linux_16: x86_64 Linux, 16 vCPU: CPU-bound jobs (compiles, linters, large test suites)
capabilities.linux_32: x86_64 Linux, 32 vCPU: the largest parallel builds and test shards
capabilities.linux_arm64: aarch64 Linux; native ARM64 package entrypoint verification
capabilities.macos_15: macOS 15 image, and therefore the macOS 15 default SDK
capabilities.macos_15_gui: macOS 15 with a foreground Aqua login session (XCUITest, virtual display)
capabilities.macos_15_sdk15: macOS 15 carrying an SDK 15 Xcode alongside the pinned one
capabilities.macos_26_ios: macOS 26 with installed iOS runtimes and a working simctl
capabilities.macos_26_large: macOS 26 on the large SKU: 12 vCPU, 48 GB RAM, 250 GB disk

$comment: What kind of work a job does, and whether that work needs macOS.
scripts/ci/runner_routing_table.py fails a macOS job with no macos_jobs entry,
and a macOS job whose class needs linux (unless it is an existing job with a
linux_followup). See docs/ci-runner-capability-map.md.

apple-app-build.description: Builds the macOS app, an Apple framework or an xcframework with Xcode or SwiftPM against AppKit, SwiftUI or WebKit, or seeds those builds' caches.

apple-swift-tests.description: Swift tests of packages that import Darwin, Foundation networking, CryptoKit, Security, AppKit or another Apple-only framework.

apple-gui.description: Needs a macOS login session or window server: UI tests, app-host tests, captures, tours, frame benchmarks.

apple-ios.description: iOS builds, simulators and App Store Connect tooling.

apple-signing-release.description: Signs, notarizes, staples, verifies or publishes Apple release artifacts with codesign, notarytool or the keychain.

macos-runtime-tests.description: Tests how code behaves on macOS itself: PTYs, launchd, the system keychain, the network stack, an Intel run-time check, a built binary launched on macOS.

rust-darwin-release-build.description: Release builds of the Rust macOS targets that link against the real Apple SDK and package npm and PyPI. Compile-only checks of those targets are rust-darwin-compile.

rust-darwin-compile.description: Compiles the Rust macOS targets without running them; scripts/ci/macos-cross.sh does this on Linux (darwin_builder: linux).

cpp-unit-tests.description: Compiles and runs C or C++ unit tests that use only the standard library; clang++ on Linux runs them.

shell-parse.description: Parses or lints shell scripts, including with a specific bash version, which can be built on Linux.

portable-swift-packages.description: Swift packages that build without Apple-only frameworks; swift test runs them on Linux.

web-and-tooling.description: TypeScript, JavaScript, Python or Rust tests, linters, formatters and generators that do not call Apple tools.

portable-checks.description: Static checks and stdlib Python, bash and bun tests that run the same on Linux and macOS: fleet Linux first, then a free owned mini with no nightly job waiting, Blacksmith Linux last (scripts/ci/portable_job_placement.py).

$comment: Every job whose runs-on can route to macOS, as <workflow file>#<job id> -> job class.
A new macOS job adds its line here and takes its owned-pool label from placement.
linux_followup marks an existing job that should move to Linux; placement_followup an existing
job that reads the side-lane label variable directly; picker_followup an existing job whose runs-on
reads no picker output and so waits on one fixed label (scripts/ci/runner_routing_table.py). All three
lists only shrink.

$comment: allowed_secrets names every secret each job may reference, including inherited workflow env; omitted means none.
Same-repository nightly jobs may use GitHub-hosted Ubuntu only during their declared bootstrap route.

The route still prefers a verified fleet reservation and measured Blacksmith overflow; this table never permits release/signing operations, credentialed visual-gate routing or artifact publication on hosted Ubuntu.
The Blacksmith Linux size of every job that named blacksmith-32vcpu-ubuntu-2404 on 2026-11-01,
with the measurement that picked it (Leo, 2026-11-01, on 1,531 jobs queued on 32 vCPU: "ok. we clearly
are not able to use them. so we should have resized a long-ass time ago."). Blacksmith caps concurrency
in vCPUs, so one 32 vCPU job holds the room of eight 4 vCPU jobs. Fleet routes (portable placement, a
non-Blacksmith LINUX_RUNNER, owned Macs) still come first; this sizes only the Blacksmith overflow member.
`size` is the job's Blacksmith label, `failover` the size it takes while CI_CLOUD_OVERFLOW_SAVED is set.
`measured` maps a vCPU size to [runs per day, mean wall minutes, p90 wall minutes] from `measured_from`.
A size of 32 needs `why_32`. A `pending` job still routes to 32 until the open pull request it names lands;
`target` is the size it moves to. tests/test_ci_blacksmith_linux_sizes.py fails any runs-on that can resolve
to 32 vCPU without an entry here, and a `pending` list that grows.
linux_sizes.prices_source: `blacksmith runners catalog` (cmuxterm-hq build-fleet/swift-linux-builder/blacksmith/RESULTS.md): $0.004/min at 2 vCPU and $0.064/min at 32, linear in vCPUs; billing rounds each job up to a whole minute
linux_sizes.measured_from: cmuxterm-hq build-fleet/data speed records for 2026-10-30 and 2026-10-31: every Blacksmith job's label and wall time
